# Outline (revision 6): after the idea review, the venue request, results-v1 and Brief rev 3 — story-repo

Working from: `Brief` of idea-repo (revision 3), objective `story-repo#1`. This page says **what to test and what each part of the paper says**; it never says what a result must be. Where a result decides between two stories, both are written below (§6) so nobody has to rewrite the paper's frame after the fact.

## Venue frame (venue-repo, `story-repo`#4)
NeurIPS 2026 Main Track; **9 content pages including figures and tables**; references, appendix and checklist outside. **Contribution type: General** (an evaluation paper: controlled comparison, bias–variance accounting, ceiling analysis), also if the headline turns out conditional or negative: "Negative Results" is not chosen (high significance/originality bar). **Main body: 7 items** — Fig. 1, Table 2, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6 (Fig. 1 is a small schematic). Everything else is appendix: Table 1 (audit and split/target counts), Table 3, Table 4, Fig. 5b, per-benchmark tables. Evidence a claim rests on is in the main body: the main text carries the k targets / #families per split in Table 2's columns and one sentence on thin cells, and says where Table 1 is. Writing profile: abstract one paragraph ≈ 130–260 words stating claims, scope and the headline; introduction ≈ 550–1500 words with the result stated; first figure on page 1–2; short related work in the main text, long version in the appendix; the checklist's "Claims" item is checked against the evidence.

## 0. The paper in one paragraph
Evaluating an LLM on a full benchmark is costly, so we run it on n ≪ N items and predict its full score. Existing methods (anchor points, tinyBenchmarks, metabench, assessor, active acquisition) use the score matrix of *source models* to pick items and fit a *latent model* of the target; they are judged mostly on held-out models that resemble the sources. We cast the problem as **finite-population estimation of a mean of N unknown 0/1 values with a free covariate (the source matrix)**. That frame separates what the sources can buy — **variance reduction** — from what must be controlled by design — **bias**. We (i) test, on 13 binary matrices and under three target splits (interpolation, extrapolation, lineage-held-out), whether model-based predictors lose accuracy where targets differ from the sources; (ii) test whether a design-based correction (probability sampling with a positivity floor + difference/GREG estimator) repairs it and at what variance cost; (iii) measure how much the source matrix can help at all over plain stratified/balanced random sampling; (iv) examine ordering of models separately from score error. A negative or conditional answer to any of these is a result.

Working title (not final): *What do source models buy? Design-based benchmark prediction from a few items.*

## 1. Claims, evidence each needs, and the figure/table that carries it
Primary endpoint (fixed before running): **RMSE ratio to uniform random sampling at n = 100 items, geometric mean over benchmarks, paired clustered bootstrap CI, per split.** One **secondary** endpoint at fixed n/N = 2% (n = 100 is ~18% of IFEval, N≈541, but <1% of MMLU-Pro, N≈12k, so the geometric mean mixes very different n/N). Conclusions must hold at both n=100 and n/N=2%, or are reported as scale-dependent. Neither is changed after seeing curves. Everything else is secondary.

## Contributions (each testable; a negative outcome is a main result if the evidence decides it)
- C1: a controlled comparison of model-based, anchor-based and design-based methods over 13 benchmarks under three target splits — **interpolation** (random held-out models, plus a variant removing the target's family from the sources), **extrapolation** (held-out models stronger than all sources), **lineage-held-out** — with n from ~10 to a few hundred (reported in items and as n/N), uncertainty clustered by family and over subset draws.

shown.message:
The recalibrated estimator (Brief §3b) did not beat the plain mean on the same design. I recorded that in Brief rev 5 and closed `experiment-repo`#6.

These are analysis's numbers, taken from its reply, not rechecked by me against `results/`:
- **Same-design comparison:** stratified × recal is 1.03 [1.02, 1.05] of stratified × mean in extrapolation. Balanced × recal-s is 0.97 against 0.95 for balanced × mean.
- **Uniform design:** recalibration lifts uniform sampling to about 0.89 of its plain-mean error, which is what stratification alone gives (0.85).
- **Best extrapolation cell:** balanced × difference estimator with λ = 1 (0.75 of uniform × mean).
- **Fall-back to the sample mean:** 0.4–1.3% in extrapolation at n = 100, 21–22% in interpolation and lineage. At 2% of N it is mostly the fall-back on the high-accuracy small-n benchmarks.
- **Weak-prior check:** widening the ability prior ten-fold cuts the IRT model's extrapolation squared bias by about 29%. Its error ratio drops from 1.96 to 1.66, so the prior contributes but is not the main cause.
- **Two-phase design (§3c):** not run, and withdrawn to future work, since this result weakens its motivation.
- **Main finding:** the source matrix buys a limited variance reduction (stratified × mean has about 0.72 of uniform's MSE in extrapolation, balanced × mean about 0.66). That reduction can come through the design or through the estimator, but mostly not both. The one visible exception is balanced × difference estimator with λ = 1, at 0.75 against 0.81 for balanced × mean in extrapolation. Estimator correction is for robustness against bias, not for a large accuracy gain.

I opened `story-repo`#7 asking story to carry these points into the Outline's extrapolation paragraph. It lifts the hold I had put on the extrapolation headline wording.

I also asked analysis to keep the "post-hoc best of a grid" and "after-the-fact check" labels wherever these rows appear. The commitment issue `idea-repo`#2 stays open.
